title: Nobody names their son “Perez” hoping he becomes a sermon.
paragraphs: Nobody names their son “Perez” hoping he becomes a sermon.

Most believers rush past his name like it is background noise in the genealogy of Jesus. Just another ancient figure buried inside a long list of impossible Hebrew names. But heaven does not waste ink.
Perez appears in moments that feel almost hidden… yet God places him directly inside the bloodline of Christ.
That should make us stop.

Because Perez was born from scandal.
From brokenness.
From confusion.
From a story many churches would rather skip quickly.
And yet God did not erase him.
He highlighted him.

The name “Perez” in Hebrew is פֶּרֶץ (Perets or Perez), coming from the root פָּרַץ (parats), meaning:
“to break through,”
“to burst forth,”
“to breach.”

This was not a quiet birth.
This was disruption.

In Genesis 38, Tamar is giving birth to twins. One child stretches out his hand first, and the midwife ties a scarlet thread around it. But then suddenly he pulls back, and the other child violently breaks through first.
Genesis 38:29 says:
“וַיְהִי כְּמֵשִׁיב יָדוֹ וְהִנֵּה יָצָא אָחִיו וַתֹּאמֶר מַה־פָּרַצְתָּ עָלֶיךָ פָּרֶץ”
Transliterated:
“Vayehi k’meshiv yado v’hineh yatza achiv vatomer mah-paratzta alekha paretz.”
A deeply literal rendering says:
“But as he drew back his hand, behold, his brother came out, and she said, ‘What a breach you have made for yourself!’ Therefore his name was called Perez.”
A breach.
A breakthrough.
An interruption of expected order.
Perez was not supposed to emerge first.
But heaven had already chosen the line.
That alone preaches louder than most people realize.

Because some of you have spent your whole life believing you came second.
Second choice.
Second best.
Second in line.
Second in approval.
Second in worth.
Second in opportunity.
Second in spiritual maturity.
But God specializes in overturning human expectation.

Abel over Cain.
Isaac over Ishmael.
Jacob over Esau.
Joseph over his brothers.
David over all his older brothers.

And Perez…
over the hand with the scarlet thread.
The scarlet-threaded child looked like the obvious promise.
But appearances deceive.
God often chooses the overlooked breakthrough.
And this story becomes even heavier when you realize where Perez came from.

Judah had failed morally.
Tamar had been abandoned and mistreated.
The entire chapter feels uncomfortable, messy, morally complex, and emotionally raw.
Most people reading Genesis 38 feel tempted to rush through it.
But Matthew refuses to skip it.
Matthew 1:3 says:
“Ἰούδας δὲ ἐγέννησεν τὸν Φαρὲς καὶ τὸν Ζάρα ἐκ τῆς Θαμάρ”
Transliterated Greek:
“Ioudas de egennēsen ton Phares kai ton Zara ek tēs Thamar.”
Literal rendering:
“Judah fathered Perez and Zerah by Tamar.”
By Tamar.
Matthew intentionally leaves her name there.
Why?
Because the Gospel never hides the scandal grace overcame.

Religion edits messy people out.
Jesus writes them into His genealogy.
That is one of the most powerful realities in Scripture.
The bloodline of Christ contains prostitutes, adulterers, failures, outsiders, liars, broken kings, and scandal-covered stories.

Not because God celebrates sin…
but because He redeems sinners.
Perez becomes proof that your beginning does not cancel God’s purpose.

Somebody reading this still secretly believes:
“My story disqualified me.”
But the genealogy of Jesus destroys that lie.
Perez was born through a situation filled with shame, tension, grief, and public humiliation.

Yet God looked at that child and said:
“Through this line, My Son will come.”
Read that again slowly.
The Messiah entered history through a family tree humanity would have hidden.
That is grace.

Not polished grace.
Not Instagram grace.
Not church-performance grace.
Real grace.

The kind that walks directly into broken bloodlines and says:
“I can still bring redemption from this.”
And maybe that is why Perez matters more than we realized.
Because spiritually, Perez represents breakthrough after shame.
Breakthrough after rejection.
Breakthrough after hidden grief.
Breakthrough after generations of dysfunction.
The Hebrew root פָּרַץ (parats) appears throughout Scripture in moments of violent breakthrough.
In Micah 2:13, speaking prophetically:
“עָלָה הַפֹּרֵץ לִפְנֵיהֶם”
“The Breaker goes up before them.”
“The One who breaks through goes before them.”
Jewish scholars often connected this imagery to divine deliverance — God Himself breaking impossible barriers for His people.
Perez carries that same language in his very name.
A breaker-through.
And isn’t that exactly what Jesus became?

The One who broke through sin.
Broke through death.
Broke through the veil.
Broke through hopelessness.
Broke through the separation between God and man.
Even the veil in the Temple was torn open.

Not gently opened.
Torn.
A breach.
Perez was whispering something prophetic generations before Bethlehem.
God’s redemption would come through breakthrough.
And maybe the reason so many people overlook Perez is because we are uncomfortable with how God works.

We prefer clean stories.
Predictable stories.
Safe stories.
But heaven keeps choosing unlikely people.

The overlooked son.
The abandoned woman.
The disgraced family line.
The failed disciple.
The former persecutor.
The thief on the cross.

And somewhere in all of that…
God keeps rewriting endings.

That means your failure is not final.
Your shame is not sovereign.
Your past is not your permanent identity.

If Christ can come through Perez…
then God can still bring purpose through you.
Somebody needed that today more than they want to admit.
Be honest.
You have smiled publicly while privately believing your mistakes were louder than God’s calling.
But Perez stands inside the genealogy of Jesus like a holy contradiction against despair.
A reminder that grace does not avoid broken stories.
It enters them.

And maybe the character you almost overlooked…
was actually carrying a message about your own life.
You thought God forgot you because your story became messy.
But heaven has always specialized in breakthrough births.

The bloodline of Jesus was never proof that humanity was worthy of Him…
it was proof that His grace was willing to enter humanity anyway.
